snippet: ## GENERAL POLICIES ## Sustainable Purchasing Policy of the Acerinox Group ### February 26, 2025 TABLE OF CONTENTS I) INTRODUCTION AND PURPOSE 2 II) SCOPE OF APPLICATION 2 III) PURPOSES 2 IV) GENERAL PRINCIPLES 3 V) GOVERNANCE 4 VI) POLICY DISSEMINATION 4 VII) REVIEW, UPDATING, AND IMPLEMENTATION 5 I) INTRODUCTION AND PURPOSE The Board of Directors of Acerinox, S.A. (hereinafter, “Acerinox” or the “Company”), as a listed company, holds the legally non-delegable authority to establish the general policies and strategies of the Company and of the Group of which it is the parent company. This Sustainable Purchasing Policy of the Acerinox Group (hereinafter, the “Policy”) aims to set out guidelines for Acerinox and its Group entities on purchasing goods and contracting services within the Group's activities, to encourage best practices in sustainability. This Policy aligns with the Code of Conduct and Good Practices of Acerinox S.A. and its Group of companies, the Code of Conduct for Business Partners of the Acerinox Group, the General Sustainability Policy of the Acerinox Group, and specifically, the Sustainability Due Diligence Policy. It also adheres to international norms and standards on sustainability. In accordance with the foregoing, the Acerinox Board of Directors approved this Policy during its meeting on February 26, 2025. II) SCOPE OF APPLICATION This Policy applies to Acerinox and entities within the Acerinox Group (hereinafter, the “Acerinox Group” or the “Group”) and, as such, is applicable to all its directors, managers, and employees. Subsidiaries may develop their own rules, which must comply with this Policy and other internal regulations set by Acerinox affecting the Group, while also considering the specific legal requirements of the markets in which they operate. Subsidiaries are required to provide all necessary information to the Company and cooperate to ensure the effective implementation of this Policy. The different entities within the Group will ensure that the principles of the Policy are applied, where appropriate and to the extent applicable, to the individuals or legal entities that have commercial relationships with any of the entities comprising the Acerinox Group (hereinafter, the “Business Partners”) throughout their chain of activities (hereinafter, the “Activity Chain”). For entities not controlled by Acerinox and its subsidiaries, the promotion of principles that align with this Policy will be encouraged. Where relevant, this Policy also applies to joint ventures, temporary business associations, and similar partnerships where Acerinox or its subsidiaries take on a management role. III) PURPOSES The Acerinox Group aims to be a leader in sustainability by incorporating ethical principles into its business model and promoting sustainable practices in all its contracting processes. BUSINESS MODEL Acerinox is one of the world’s most competitive stainless steel manufacturers and the most global company in the market. Its business objective is the production and sale of stainless steel and, with this purpose, from its very foundation, the company has developed a continuous investment programme, often with the development of its own technological innovations which, in certain cases, have involved real milestones in the field of stainless steel technology. Acerinox is one of the largest manufacturers worldwide thanks to its six plants in four different continents in which flat and long products are manufactured. Three plants are integral (including steelworks, hot rolling and cold rolling). These are Acerinox Europe (Campo de Gibraltar, Spain), North American Stainless (Kentucky, USA), and Columbus Stainless (Middelburg, South Africa). The fourth big plant, Bahru Stainless (Johor Bahru, Malaysia) has a cold rolling mill. In addition, for the manufacturing of long products, Acerinox also has the plants at Roldan (Ponferrada, Spain) and Inoxfil (Igualada, Spain). Non-Financial Information Record 2018 4 The main shareholders of the Acerinox Group are Corporación Financiera Alba (18.96%), Nisshin Steel Co. Ltd (15.49%), Omega Capital (5.0%), and IDC (Industrial Development Corporation) (3.19%). The Acerinox Group has a sales structure which is present in 56 countries, from which it sells stainless steel to a total of 86 countries across 5 continents. This structure is made up of 18 service centres, 26 warehouses, and 35 sales offices, not to mention the countless sales agents in various countries which do not have a permanent office. Thanks to this structure and to the excellence in operations and product quality, the Acerinox Group is the leader in one of the continents, Africa, in addition to being the largest producer in the world’s largest economy, the United States, and having large market shares in all the geographical areas in which it operates. Acerinox employees have good working conditions, higher than the industry average pay, 93% of workers have permanent contracts, stable and high-quality jobs, training courses, international projection and a wide range of possibilities to develop a long and rewarding professional career within the company. The Model has as the ultimate objective of providing reasonable security for attaining objectives, whether strategic, operational, compliance, or reporting. For the correct implementation of the measures and the strict monitoring of its fulfilment of them in each of the possible risks, in 2015 the Group approved the Risk Management Control Policy of Acerinox, S.A., and their Group of Companies. Through the Policy, the mechanisms and basic principles are established for the management of opportunities and risks that allow them to:  Achieve the strategic objectives determined by the Group.  Provide full guarantees for the shareholders.  Protect the Group’s results and reputation.  Defend the interests of the key Interest Groups of the Company.  Ensure business stability and financial solidity in a sustained manner over time. Any business activity generally has a series of risks associated to it and, in the case of steel making, Acerinox recognises and classifies the uncertainties characteristic of the industry in which it operates. Non-Financial Information Record 2018 8 3. ENVIRONMENTAL MATTERS 3.1 Environmental Matters Sustainability and taking care of the environment are among the priorities of the company, and Acerinox understands their importance for an organisation that has the intention to maintain its position and endure into the future. Acerinox is committed to the environment and its surrounding areas, to reducing environmental impact during the production process, to collaborating with the communities in which it operates and, of course, to its employees and stakeholders. This effort has been recognised by organisations such as FTSE4Good, which includes the Acerinox Group in its global assessment index of responsible companies that demonstrate their application of solid environmental measures and corporate social responsibility and recognises companies who work towards environmental sustainability. Non-Financial Information Record 2018 9 During the development of production and waste management, the precautionary principle against environmental risks is applied along with measures to prevent and, if necessary, react quickly to a potential hazard to health or the environment. The environmental risks are contained in the operational risks section of Acerinox, S.A.’s Risk Control and Management Policy. Acerinox’s activity requires large energy consumption and emissions are linked to its productive capacity. Therefore, the company’s efforts are aimed at reducing emissions and putting the most suitable filters in place before allowing these emissions to be released. In this task, the reduction of CO2 emissions implies a constant commitment, both from Acerinox itself, and from a sustainable industry which is committed to the fight against climate change. Additionally, stainless steel is a metal that is recycled almost in its entirety and indefinitely, so it is indefinitely reusable and requires much less energy to manufacture than other similar materials, such as aluminium or titanium; also, it does not require chemicals for its correct storage. The main raw material for the manufacture of stainless steel in our plants comes from scrap; therefore, Acerinox is one of the largest recyclers of this waste product in all the countries in which it has steelworks. The areas of application of stainless steel are almost unlimited and demand has steadily and increasingly grown in recent decades, with rates of increase of an average of approximately 6% each year, it is also a fundamental pillar of the circular economy. The applications of stainless steel include quite a few utilities related to the environment such as generating clean energy and saving on energy consumption, providing clean air, water treatment, producing healthy food, avoiding hazardous chemicals and limiting environmental pollution. With regards to the environmental provisions, the Group has not registered any environmental provisions for 2018. Non-Financial Information Record 2018 10 3.2 Climate Change As mentioned in the first point of this report, Acerinox is recognised in the global Carbon Disclosure Project (CDP) and is included in the B List of leading companies in the fight against climate change through the implementation of activities to reduce emissions and minimise the risks of the organisation in relation to climate change. The Group is well-aware of the Sustainable Development Goals of the European Union, including the fight against climate change and the effects resulting from it. At Acerinox we are committed to maintaining scrupulous care of the environment surrounding our production facilities and offices, to continue investing in research and technology to reduce energy consumption and emissions from our activities and waste as much as possible, to defend and promote respect for biodiversity in all its aspects and to strengthen the role of Corporate Social Responsibility within the Group and the companies which form it. 3.3 Pollution The manufacturing process for stainless steel requires an intensive use of energy. The Acerinox Group is strongly committed to reducing energy consumption and CO2 emissions. To do this, all operations are characterised for their operational excellence, in pursuit of technological efficiency and continuous optimisation of the facilities, making Acerinox one of the most efficient companies in its commitment to the reduction of emissions, according to the International Stainless Steel Forum (ISSF). The Acerinox Group plants have strict measures in place to prevent, avoid, and resolve spillages from tipping or storing substances. The Group’s production activities are subject to strict emission controls, as well as the fulfilment of yearly objectives. In 2020, the period for recording the Greenhouse Gas Emissions (GHG) comes to an end in Europe and over the next few years the rights to free emissions are going to be reduced. By following the recommendations from the various international regulations, the Acerinox Group can calculate the direct and indirect emissions. Acerinox has control, measurement, and gas filtering systems in all of its equipment and takes special care to comply in this field. Proof of this is found in the fact that in order to reduce NOx emissions, the plants have catalytic NOx emissions Non-Financial Information Record 2018 11 towers, where NOx vapours are converted into molecular nitrogen, so that the NOx emissions are well below the strict legal limits. The company is aware that through its Zero Emissions Target programme, a conception of environmental policy entails the constant target of reducing all emissions to the extent possible, in absolute terms and in relative terms or specific ones. The ZET is a constant battle which stems from the Company’s own initiative, rather than from a regulatory imperative. The Acerinox Group plants have strict measures in place to prevent, avoid, and resolve spillages from tipping or storing substances. All the plants have neutralisation plants for treating acidic and basic waste water as well as emergency dams and other security mechanisms for containing any possible spillages. Similarly, the tanks are also equipped with a rigid inner tank, with an emergency stop function and an emergency cleaning service. The manufacturing process of stainless steel at Acerinox begins with the melting of scrap (primarily) which, after treatment and the application of the necessary processes, becomes a metal which has many different applications in various industries and, with proper maintenance, it has a useful lifespan which can last for centuries and which leaves a considerably smaller footprint than other alloy emissions. In economic terms, it converts a product of little value into one of great value that will be recycled once again at the end of its useful life, creating jobs in the process, taking care of the environment and thereby polluting the planet even less, thereby closing the perfect economic circle. In order to do this, Acerinox maintains a continuous and two-way dialogue with public bodies and authorities, governments and other local concerned parties, following the guidelines set out in the Code of Conduct and Best Practices of the company. With regards to job creation, during 2018 there have been 598 new incorporations bringing the Group’s workforce to a total of 6,709 employees. The impact of the activity of our company on employment and local development in the areas in which it operates is very significant, it being one of the main generators of stable and quality employment. The payment of salaries, amounts paid in taxes and social security and the indirect activity generated by its plants are one of the leading producers of wealth and a social stabiliser. Each of the companies which make up the Group has its own established communication channels through which it can apply to cooperate with social action programmes. In each of these there are managers for this department whose telephone numbers and email addresses are available in order for them to be able to answer these requests. Following the internal regulations, any request that requires processing must be submitted in writing, specifying the amount of the request, the object for which it is intended, the organisation that has requested it and the channels through which it can be undertaken. In each case, a commission is responsible for assessing all the requests and for the granting of those considered most necessary. 7.2 Subcontracting and Suppliers In order to ensure a stable, sustainable supply chain, the company has fundamental tools such as the Code of Conduct and the accreditation processes of each factory, in order to verify the requirements they must meet in respect of health and safety, employment and environmental practices, among others. Process Safety Key Performance Indicators​ 30 1 Uncontrolled copy Process Safety Framework Code: ESG-OM-17 Edition: 0 Code: ESG-OM-17 Edition: 0 Date:July 23rd 2025 Produced by: Digitally Signed: Name: Nicole Hijón Tankovics Position: HSE Specialist Reviewed by: Digitally Signed: Name: Jose Campuzano Talavera Position: Global HSE Director Approved by: Digitally Signed: Name: Bernardo Velazquez Herreros Position: CEO REVISION nº MODIFICATIONS ON THE PREVIOUS REVISION MODIFICATION DATE Draft Issued for comments June 23rd-2025 0 Issued document July 23rd 2025 2 Uncontrolled copy Process Safety Framework Code: ESG-OM-17 Edition: 0 1.​ Purpose The purpose of this General Method is to standardize the Process Safety Management concepts across the Acerinox worksites and operations to: ●​ Avoid loss of containment of chemicals with potentially serious consequences for people, environment and assets ●​ Enhance risk awareness and personal behaviors in operations involving hazardous chemicals and processes. 2.​ Scope This General Method applies to all Acerinox operations within Acerinox premises. Share and promote this General Method with co-workers and Service Contractors during safety meetings and talks, field visits and other opportunities to communicate with work teams. Contact your Business Unit HSE managers if you have any questions regarding the application of this General Method. 3.​ Definitions Explosion A release of energy that causes a pressure discontinuity or blast wave (e.g. detonations, deflagrations, and rapid releases of high pressure caused by rupture of equipment or piping). Fire Any combustion resulting from a LOPC, regardless of the presence of flame. This includes smouldering, charring, smoking, singeing, scorching, carbonizing, or the evidence that any of these have occurred. Loss of primary containment (LOPC) An unplanned or uncontrolled release of any material from its primary containment, including non-toxic and non-flammable materials (e.g. steam, hot water, nitrogen, compressed CO2, or compressed air). Molten Metal / Molten Slag The manufacture of steel and its by-products involves the use of various metals, ferroalloys, and fluxes, such as stainless steel, carbon steel, iron ore, steel mills, fluorspar, etc. 3 Uncontrolled copy Process Safety Framework Code: ESG-OM-17 Edition: 0 As well as the handling of the resulting molten slag. Primary Containment A tank, vessel, pipe, truck, rail car, or other equipment designed to keep material within it – typically for the purposes of storage, separation, processing, or transfer of material. Process Production, distribution, storage, utilities, or pilot plant facilities used in the manufacture of steel products and co-products. This includes process equipment (e.g. reactors, vessels, piping, electric arc furnaces, blast furnaces, coke ovens, boilers, pumps, compressors, exchangers, cooling towers, refrigeration systems, etc.), storage tanks, ancillary support areas (e.g. boiler houses and waste water treatment plants), on-site remediation facilities, and distribution piping under control of the company. Process Safety Management Process safety management (PSM) is a blend of engineering, operations and management skills focused on preventing catastrophic accidents, particularly structural collapse, explosions, fires and toxic releases associated with loss of containment of energy or dangerous substances such as toxic gases, molten metal, chemicals and petroleum products. For Acerinox, uncontrolled releases of molten steel from vessels and process lines, as well as uncontrolled releases of solid metal from process lines may result in severe damage to human health and surrounding assets and are to be included as process safety management events. Safety-Critical Equipment (SCE) A specific piece of hardware or a device designed to perform a particular safety function. Its failure could directly lead to a hazardous situation (e.g.: Emergency shutdown valves, Pressure relief Valves, PSVs, Fire suppression systems). Safety-Critical Systems (SCS) A collection of interconnected components (which may include safety-critical equipment) working together to ensure safety. It's a more complex entity with multiple layers of protection (e.g.:EAF tilting control systems, storage tank farm Level Controls). Secondary Containment An impermeable physical barrier specifically designed to mitigate the impact of materials that have breached primary containment. 4 Uncontrolled copy Process Safety Framework Code: ESG-OM-17 Edition: 0 Secondary Containments must not be accounted as direct barriers that avoid LOPC. Secondary containment systems include, but are not limited to tank dikes, curbing around process equipment, drainage collection systems, the outer wall of open top double walled tanks, etc. ACRONYMS ADN: European Agreement concerning the International Carriage of Dangerous Goods by Inland Waterways ADR: European Agreement concerning the International Carriage of Dangerous Goods by Road. BUs: Business Units CCPS: Center Chemical Process Safety EAF: Electric Arc Furnace EPSC: European Process Safety Center HAZOP: Hazard and Operability Study HSE: Health, Safety, Environment IOGP: International Association of Oil and Gas Producers LO(TO)2: Lock Out, Tag Out, Try Out LOPC: Loss of Primary Containment MoC: Management of Change LO(TO)2: Lock Out, Tag Out, Try Out P&ID: Diagrama de Tuberias e Instrumentación PS: Process Safety PPE: Personal Protective Equipment PSM: Process Safety Management RIS: Regulations concerning the International Carriage of Dangerous Goods by Rail 5 Uncontrolled copy Process Safety Framework Code: ESG-OM-17 Edition: 0 SWA: Stop Work Authority WS: World Steel Association 4.​ Process Safety Framework Manufacturing processes of Stainless Steel and High Performance Alloys involves processes of intrinsic operational, product and energy source hazards that need detailed and careful management. The measures needed to control these hazards are complex and go beyond protecting the people but also includes the environment, assets and surrounding community. Based on the World Steel Process Safety Fundamentals, Acerinox Group has defined various cross functional processes to support the implementation of a Risk based approach to Process Safety Management, rather than a compliance based. This helps the group to allocate resources focusing on high-risk activities. Additionally, and as a complement to the Cardinal Rules (ESG-OM-14), Acerinox has defined a set of Process Safety Principles which are intended to support frontline workers, supervisors and operational management to focus their attention into situations that could lead to a release of a hazardous chemical or energy with potential for severe consequence. Acerinox Group Process Safety Principles are based on best industry practices: ●​ Process Safety Fundamentals from World Steel 6 Uncontrolled copy Process Safety Framework Code: ESG-OM-17 Edition: 0 ●​ Process Safety Fundamentals from European Process Safety Centre (EPSC) ●​ Process Safety Standards from American Petroleum Institute (API) ●​ Golden Rules and Key Principles from Center ChemicalProcess Safety (CCPS) 7 Uncontrolled copy Process Safety Framework Code: ESG-OM-17 Edition: 0 4.1.​ Acerinox Process Safety Principles Handle Molten Metal Hazard Uncontrolled release of molten metal, leading to severe burns, fires, explosions, and environmental contamination. Main Energy sources, temperature, gravity, motion, mechanical, chemical and electrical When is this important? ●​ During loading of basket with raw material ●​ During the transfer of molten metal between vessels or equipment. ●​ During the casting or pouring of molten metal. ●​ During maintenance or repair activities on equipment containing molten metal. ●​ During the transportation of molten metal via road carriers. ●​ During the decanting of molten metal from one ladle to another. ●​ During deslagging operations in slag cones, transport of slag cones, tipping of cones in the slagging area, handling of slag in slag ponds, as well as cooling of slag before being treated. Challenges in the Field ●​ Failure to wear or maintain appropriate PPE for high-temperature environments. ●​ Degradation or failure of refractory linings and other containment systems. ●​ Presence of uncontrolled ignition sources near molten metal operations. ●​ Inadequate or poorly practiced emergency response procedures for molten metal spills or releases. ●​ Securing ladles and carriers properly during transportation to prevent shifting and spillage. ●​ Condition of roads for transport. ●​ Liquid coming in contact with molten metal causing explosions. ●​ Inadequate route planning and monitoring when using public roads. ●​ Mechanical condition of carriers and equipment ●​ Ensuring safe and controlled decanting operations to prevent spills and splashes. ●​ Coordinating activities between personnel involved in decanting operations. ●​ Observe the safe filling level for slag removal ladles and cones to avoid overflows and splashes. 8 Uncontrolled copy Process Safety Framework Code: ESG-OM-17 Edition: 0 ●​ Water must not leak into the cooling hoods and fume extraction ducts, as well as into the cooled vaults of electric furnaces and their cooling panels. ●​ A small amount of water or even moisture on the floor (e.g., moist/hydrated lime dust) also constitutes an explosion risk. furnaces or ladles. ●​ Prevent closed containers from being loaded in the charge basket ●​ Ensure slag tip stations are free from liquid accumulation before tipping ●​ Provide specialized training for Implement engineering controls to minimize the risk of spills and releases, such as automated transfer systems and overflow containment. ●​ Develop and practice emergency response plans for molten When is it Important? ●​ During loading of basket with raw material ●​ During the transfer of molten metal between vessels or equipment. ●​ During the casting or pouring of molten metal. ●​ During the addition of scrap as setting and/or cooling material in AOD converter and/or ladles. ●​ During maintenance or repair activities on equipment containing molten metal. ●​ During the transportation of molten metal via road carriers. ●​ During the decanting of molten metal from one ladle to another. Challenges in the Field ●​ Scrap Storage, open-air scrap yards are vulnerable to rain and snow, which can saturate the scrap. ●​ Trapped Water, certain types of scrap, such as hollow objects or those with complex shapes, trap water, making difficult to detect. ●​ Ice, in cold climates, ice can form on scrap, and can be harder to detect than liquid water. ●​ Storage parks must be built with a concrete base. Preventive Measures ●​ Improved storage, by utilizing covered storage areas or sheds to protect scrap from rain and snow, whenever posible. ●​ Ensure proper drainage in scrap yards to prevent water accumulation. ●​ Organize scrap piles to allow for better air circulation and drying. ●​ Enhanced inspections and develop strict scrap inspection protocols to identify and reject wet scrap. ●​ Train personnel on the hazards of wet scrap and proper safety procedures. ●​ Ensure that all personnel in the EAF area wear appropriate PPE, including heat-resistant clothing, face shields, and helmets. ●​ Develop and maintain detailed Emergency Response Plans for handling explosions and other incidents. ●​ Establish clear evacuation procedures and assembly points. ●​ Enforce a culture of strict adherence to safety procedures and protocols. ●​ Thoroughly investigate all incidents and near-misses to identify root causes and implement corrective actions. ●​ Conduct regular safety audits to Process Safety Framework Code: ESG-OM-17 Edition: 0 Avoid Rolling Mill Cobbles Hazards During the hot rolling process, the bar/billet/slabs can come out of the line's boxes and paths, generating cobbles at over 1000 ºC. This uncontrolled situation can cause fires, material damage and personal injury. When is it important? The activation of scrapping by shears in certain areas may not be enough to prevent the bar from reaching risk areas such as hydraulic power plants or electrical installations. In addition, in the block, and at the entry and exit points of the loop former, the speed of the bar can cause the material to cause damage at a great distance. Challenges in the field ●​ The complexity of adjusting the tooling and rolling boxes makes it difficult to establish ideal conditions to prevent cobbles. ●​ It is essential to keep the focus on capturing data and parameters of the rolling boxes in the process control computer (speeds, elongations, cylinder diameters, etc.) ●​ Process control personnel must remain attentive. ●​ Maintaining clean rolls and guides. It is necessary to keep the facilities clean, protected and with the oils in good condition. ●​ Limiting access to only authorized personnel, who should stay away from the tip of the bar. Preventive Measures ●​ Establish the necessary conditions in the tooling and rolling boxes to prevent the generation of cobbles due to mismatches. ●​ Verify that all adjustments (tooling, rolling boxes, process control parameters) have been made correctly using checklists. ●​ Implement regular breaks to keep staff attention. ●​ Carry out preventive maintenance and cleaning with the appropriate frequency. ●​ Provide continuous training to operators. ●​ Automate box changes to reduce human error. ●​ Use optical centering systems, preferably digital, to guide the bar before the box. ●​ Have more linear paths, avoiding changes of direction in the bar, to minimize the generation of cobbles. ●​ Observe the visual safety signs prohibiting traffic in the area where laminating is taking place. 12 Uncontrolled copy Process Safety Framework Code: ESG-OM-17 Edition: 0 Apply Double Isolation Hazards Spill of (hazardous) material can occur when a barrier (e.g.: valve, flange, cap) fails and no second barrier is in place. When is it important? During routine and special operations: draining & sampling, loading and unloading activities, utility connections. Challenges in the field ●​ Older plant designs often do not provide a double barrier. ●​ Blind flanges not put back after maintenance work. ●​ Blind flanges not installed with bolts & missing end caps. ●​ Importance of “primary containment” not fully understood. ●​ Valve handles that can be opened accidentally. ●​ Failures in the application of Lo(To)2 procedures (Cardinal Rules). Preventive Measures ●​ Do not rely on a single valve for positive isolation. ●​ Perform regular onsite inspections to check that drains are having an end cap (e.g.: blind flange, screw cap) according to pipe spec. ●​ Do not accept missing blind flanges or missing bolts on blind flanges. ●​ Report and investigate all incidents from leaking drains. ●​ Lock valve handles to avoid accidentally opening. Apply proper Lo(To)2 procedures and isolation devices (Cardinal Rules). ●​ Apply Isolation plans for the specific task, based on up-to-date information. ●​ Raise isolation concerns before the task starts and challenge when isolation plans cannot be executed. ●​ Monitor the integrity of isolations regularly and stop to reassess when change could affect an isolation integrity. ●​ Confirm leak-tightness before, during, and after reinstating equipment. 13 Uncontrolled copy Process Safety Framework Code: ESG-OM-17 Edition: 0 Empty and de-energize before line breaking Hazard Uncontrolled release of energy or a hazardous material during the opening of piping or equipment. When is it important? ●​ When unbolting, unscrewing, drilling or cutting of process equipment. ●​ While working on live equipment. Challenges in the field ●​ Working at the wrong location. ●​ Complexity of piping arrangements or break points. ●​ Double block and bleed is not possible. ●​ Plugging of vents or drains / leaking valves. ●​ Installing blind flanges and caps. ●​ Drains at the wrong location. ●​ Failure in the application of Lo(To)2 procedure (Cardinal Rules). Preventive Measures ●​ Have a validated isolation plan available, that indicates numbered isolation points in the right sequence on a P&ID ●​ Apply Lo(To)2 (Cardinal Rules) to avoid that equipment can be re energised: that is providing locks and labels ●​ Empty and clean equipment properly ●​ Check the completion of the isolation plan by an independent operator, before signing the permit to work ●​ Wear selected PPE for residual chemicals that might not be purged or drained and provide absorbents for leaking fluids ●​ Perform an onsite Risk Assessment by the operator performing the job, before opening, to validate the instrumentation reading and ensure its safe mode. ●​ Use blind flanges and caps according to pipe specification, as indicated in the isolation plan. ●​ Upon any process change, validate that isolation remains intact. 14 Uncontrolled copy Process Safety Framework Code: ESG-OM-17 Edition: 0 Monitor an open drain Hazards Unintended product release can occur during draining from a storage tank or other equipment to the atmosphere. When important ●​ When draining hydraulic oil from a tank or equipment. ●​ When removing chemicals from process equipment. ●​ When transferring chemicals to tanks, machines or equipment. Challenges in the field ●​ Distracted by other things that need attention during a long draining time. ●​ Bad weather conditions. ●​ Low visibility. ●​ Under estimation of the potential consequence of the product being transferred. ●​ The drain valve does not fully close. ●​ Inability to understand instrumentation. ●​ Malfunctioning or instrumentation. Options to get it right ●​ Identify the critical draining and chemical transferring operations on site. ●​ Limit drain size (typical to 1 inch) to limit the release rate of the hazardous chemical. ●​ Utilize spring loaded valves to assure that an operator remains present when drain time is short. ●​ Understand the draining time necessary when starting the draining process. ●​ Ensure the drain or transferring valve can be closed from a safe location. ●​ Avoid doing “something else” while monitoring a draining task. ●​ In a critical situation, first stop the draining or transferring process before leaving the operation. ●​ Stop draining and transferring operations during shift handover. 15 Uncontrolled copy Process Safety Framework Code: ESG-OM-17 Edition: 0 Manage overrides of Safety Critical Systems Hazard Insufficient safeguards are in place when a safety critical system is not working properly or is bypassed. When is it important? ●​ Failure of or unreliable Safety Critical Systems. ●​ Testing of safety interlocks. ●​ Turnaround or maintenance work. ●​ Pre Startup operations after maintenance. ●​ Commissioning, start up & shutdown. Challenges in the field ●​ Consequences are unknown. Lack of Risk awareness. ●​ Safety Critical Systems that prevent start up. ●​ Lack of knowledge of operational and Pre Start up procedures ●​ Absence of Authorizers and supervision. Options to get it right ●​ Understand the Safety Critical Systems (SCS) and identify them in the field. ●​ Obtain a formal authorization based on a risk assessment for every bypass/override. ●​ Evaluate how current activities could impact on the Safety Critical Systems. Maintain barrier health and alert supervision about any concerns. Apply Stop Work Authority. ●​ Define the criticality of the system to bypass like the SIL level. Authorisation level needs to be inline with this criticality. ●​ Identify and register bypasses in a Bypass Log, easily accessible in the pulpit or control room. ●​ Discuss active bypasses during shift handover and tool box talks. ●​ Determine process units that require shutdown when Safety Critical Systems are unavailable. ●​ Limit bypass duration, initiate a formal MoC for long term bypasses. ●​ Protect safety interlocks against easy bypassing in the field. ●​ Review bypassed functions every 24hr. ●​ Review statistics on bypassed equipment. ●​ Apply Impairment procedure for Active Fire & Gas Protection systems 16 Uncontrolled copy Process Safety Framework Code: ESG-OM-17 Edition: 0 Walk the line Hazards Spills or inadvertent mixing might occur when the transfer line is not ready for operation due to open ended lines or drains, or incorrect valving scheme (i.e., wrong valve or tank line-up). When is it important? After each change in set-up of a transfer line, e.g. start-up after shut-down, isolating equipment, change of equipment, maintenance work, draining. Challenges in the field ●​ Transfers occurring around shift change-over. ●​ Long transfer lines, not fully accessible. ●​ Distracted by “other things”. ●​ Bad weather, low visibility conditions. ●​ Pipelines or valve positions that are not easy to see. Preventive Measures ●​ Use up-to-date documentation (e.g.: P&IDs, Process Flow Diagrams, isometrics) that accurately reflect installed systems and equipment. ●​ Physically confirm the system is ready for the intended activity (e.g.: valve positions, line up of relief devices). ●​ Alert supervision to identified documentation and readiness issues before operation. ●​ Validate a correct line-up of all valves, tanks, pumps, before starting the pump / transfer. ●​ Perform a check, after pump start, to detect leaking drains, hoses, flanges or pump seals. ●​ Use P&IDs or better isometrics during line check. ●​ Label equipment in the field, like valves, pipelines and pumps to help with the field check. ●​ Tag all the bleed points and drains. ●​ Validate the transfer regularly by checking the levels of the tanks versus the calculated level from the pump flow speed. ●​ Take actions upon deviation. Apply Stop Work Authority. 17 Uncontrolled copy Process Safety Framework Code: ESG-OM-17 Edition: 0 Verify leak tightness after maintenance work Hazards When hazardous chemicals and fluids are reintroduced in pipes and equipment, these can still leak through flanges or other equipment enclosure. When is it important? After work where equipment valves and flanges have been opened. Temperature change can influence bolt tension and could create leakages. Challenges in the field ●​ Competent people when bolting. ●​ Bolting procedures. ●​ Seal tightness and gasket technical specifications. ●​ Verification competency or procedures are missing. Preventive Measures ●​ When undoing bolts, always start on the side furthest away from your body. Undo the bolts a bit at a time, always releasing diagonally opposing bolt pairs. With the nuts still in position, check whether the flange can be moved. ●​ Perform a leak test before introducing hazardous chemicals. ●​ Leak tests can be done by introducing a less hazardous gas and performing a pressure hold test; put soap bubbles on all flanges that have been opened; ultrasound measurements can detect leakages. ●​ Develop criteria for acceptance of leak test results. ●​ Develop a special procedure for the flange that was used in the leak-tightness test (the flange to be closed after the leak test). ●​ Verify proper flange bolting procedure, including torqueing. ●​ Validate and adjust bolt tension after heating-up the equipment. ●​ Select a suitable gasket material for the application and the conveyed medium. Always fit a new gasket. ●​ Use bolts, nuts and washers of the correct type, size and material as specified in the relevant standard. ●​ Record Leak Test results. 18 Uncontrolled copy Process Safety Framework Code: ESG-OM-17 Edition: 0 Avoid working behind a single valve Hazards Single valves can leak because they are not fully closed, are fouled or just leak. During working behind a single valve the valve might be accidentally opened or leak, releasing chemicals. When is it important? ●​ During and after line breaking due to a repair or maintenance activity. ●​ When the plant or line is not fully deenergized. ●​ During normal operation after routine maneuvers. ●​ Sampling points. Challenges in the field ●​ Older plant design often might not provide a second barrier or full block and bleed option to isolate equipment. ●​ Placing a blind, turning a spectacle flange. ●​ Failure in the application of Lo(To)2 procedure. Preventive Measures ●​ Realize when it is not possible to work behind double isolation. ●​ Try to remove the substance or energy in the system before starting working behind a single valve. ●​ If isolation by a single valve cannot be avoided: ○​ Validate that the single valve is not leaking e.g. at a drain point downstream of the isolation, or by a pressure gauge. ○​ Mechanically lock the isolation valve handle to avoid accidental knocking open during the task, deactivate the actuator for automated valves after checking the valve fail-safe position (application of Lo(To)2 procedure). ○​ Mount a spade or blind flange after the single valve directly after the line break. ○​ Consider if emergency responders should be in place during the line break, until the blind-flange is placed. ○​ Wear appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE) during the task. ○​ Work in pairs, apply “buddy” system. ○​ Keep working time short and avoid critical process conditions during. 19 Uncontrolled copy Process Safety Framework Code: ESG-OM-17 Edition: 0 Verify the condition of flexible hoses Hazards Hazardous fluid release due to hose failures. Wildly moving hoses at pressure release when coupling gets loose. When is it important? ●​ When using flexible hoses. ●​ When disconnecting hoses that still contain pressure or hazardous material. Challenges in the field ●​ Connections are not properly made, requiring bent or stretched hoses. ●​ No hose restraints or retentions available. ●​ No good storage location available. Preventive Measures ●​ Use the correct hose: correct material, specifications and temperature & pressure rating. ●​ Visually inspect hoses before using them and check for defects like corrosion, tear & wear or mechanical damage. ●​ Hose assemblies with hazardous fluids should be inspected periodically by an approved body and certified. ●​ Avoid hoses for highly hazardous chemicals (e.g.: HF, HNO3). ●​ Hoses should be tagged and included in the maintenance schedule. ●​ When not in use, hoses must be properly stored, with the appropriate bend radius, hanging straight down, or laying straight. Hoses must not be twisted or forced when connected. ●​ Apply the Hose Maintenance Plan ●​ Connect hoses well, follow-up on possible vibrations. If required replace hoses preventively and remove old hoses from the site. ●​ Ensure installation of hose restrains and retention in high pressure hoses. ●​ Double Check correct depressurization of hoses before disconnecting. 20 Uncontrolled copy Process Safety Framework Code: ESG-OM-17 Edition: 0 Operate within Safe Limits Hazards Hazardous reactions and releases or equipment damage can be caused when safe operating limits are exceeded. When is it important? ●​ Deviations from normal operation Transient operations, batch process, start-up / shut-down. ●​ At design changes. Challenges in the field ●​ Limits not well known or identified. ●​ MoC process not properly followed. ●​ Pushing production. Preventive Measures ●​ Establish safe operating limits for key process variables and for all operating phases, and make them visible for operators. ●​ Validate that instruments are working well. ●​ Understand the critical process parameters that can result in equipment damage and loss of containment due to deviations. ●​ Install alarms and interlocks for critical process variables. ●​ Define actions to bring the process variable back within the operation limit. ●​ Report and discuss the cause when operating limits are exceeded. ●​ Understand the chemical hazards at non-standard conditions and have a chemical compatibility matrix available. 21 Uncontrolled copy Process Safety Framework Code: ESG-OM-17 Edition: 0 Control utility systems connected to a process Hazards When utility systems are temporarily connected with a flexible hose to a process, hazardous substances can flow back into the utility system. When is it important? ●​ During inerting, cleaning and unplugging operational equipment using utilities. ●​ When taking a sample a utility is needed to purge a system. Challenges in the field ●​ Lack of knowledge. Easy availability of utility stations & hoses. ●​ Hazard studies did not identify the hazard. Preventive Measures ●​ Consider utility systems connected to a process through flex hose as a temporary installation under MoC Process. ●​ Remain aware of the hazard that utilities can be contaminated with process gasses or liquids. ●​ Understand the pressures in the systems and how they can deviate during operation. ●​ Define suitable safeguards against backflow, at least one non-return valve must be present. ●​ Remove the utility hoses from the process directly when the task is completed. ●​ Ensure that the hoses applied have the same pressure rating and chemical compatibility as the process when used in normal operation. ●​ Evaluate backflow during MoC and HAZOP studies when fixed connections exist between utilities and process units. 22 Uncontrolled copy Process Safety Framework Code: ESG-OM-17 Edition: 0 Report deficiencies on Safety Critical Equipment Hazards Safety Critical Equipment (SCE) provides a barrier to prevent or limit the effect of a major incident. When important ●​ When SCE is not working properly. ●​ When identified actuation of SCE under normal operations (Safe Mode) Challenges in the field ●​ A shutdown might be needed to repair the broken equipment. ●​ Not aware of the criticality. ●​ Unawareness of the failure – no testing. ●​ Unreadable equipment, like a fouled sight glass. Options to get it right ●​ Determine which equipment is considered as Safety Critical. ●​ Apply scheduled Preventive Maintenance to SCE. ●​ Respect regulatory inspection protocols and schedules for all SCE. ●​ Ensure workers know what equipment is Safety Critical, and understand the potential hazard. ●​ Maintain a testing protocol and frequency for SCE. ●​ Report failures or deviations on SCS (also from testing). ●​ Decide what action is appropriate, if necessary stop the operation. Implement interim mitigating measures that are approved, in case of continuing operation. ●​ Repair or replace SCE with highest priority. ●​ Analyse why equipment failed and maintain a log on critical equipment out of service. 23 Uncontrolled copy Process Safety Framework Code: ESG-OM-17 Edition: 0 Unplugging equipment Hazards Unplugging might require opening of installations that can unexpectedly result in a release of hazardous substances. When is it important? ●​ When process equipment is blocked e.g.: by fouling, polymer, corrosion, objects after maintenance. ●​ Maintenance works ●​ Batch processing Challenges in the field ●​ Unexpected severe flow restrictions. ●​ No unplugging procedure or good options. ●​ Not wanting to stop production. ●​ Failure in the application of Lo(To)2 procedure. Preventive Measures ●​ Consider to stop production before unplugging. Apply Stop Work Authority (SWA). ●​ Do not start unplugging without an approved plan that includes a hazard analysis. ●​ Understand the source and reason for plugging. ●​ Understand the hazards while unplugged and have a mitigation plan for unexpected releases. ●​ Understand that instrumentation might give misreading or that safety valves do not operate properly. ●​ Understand that opened equipment can still have pressurized hazardous material inside behind the plug. ●​ Follow Lo(To)2 procedure and “Empty and de-energize before line breaking” principles in the unplugging procedure. ●​ Always use inert gases to blow out pipelines / equipment (e.g.: Nitrogen, Argon). 24 Uncontrolled copy Process Safety Framework Code: ESG-OM-17 Edition: 0 Stay out of the Line of Fire Hazards Exposure in case of unexpected release of energy or chemicals or unexpected movement of objects like a manhole, also vacuum can become a hazard. When is it important ●​ When being in processing units that do not work at ambient pressure. ●​ Flex hoses connection/disconnection. ●​ Opening equipment, boxes, valves, manholes, etc. Challenges in the field ●​ Release points not designed well, e.g.: PSV release points that end in a pathway. ●​ Manholes (or manway) that are stuck. ●​ Heat releases from flares. Preventive Measures ●​ Identify hazardous locations around release points or below hoisted objects in the f field, e.g. by lines or colours on the floor. ●​ Understand release locations and remove yourself from the potential energy discharge path from release points like PSV’s, explosion panels and plugs under pressure. ●​ Keep people out of the heat radiation zone around a flare. ●​ Protect yourself (location of your body) when opening installations. ●​ Add physical barriers to prevent people from accidentally entering the paths. ●​ Verify that PSV’s are designed to always vent to a safe location. ●​ At flange opening, first untighten the bolts that are far away from you. 25 Uncontrolled copy Process Safety Framework Code: ESG-OM-17 Edition: 0 Control (un)loading Hazards Unexpected run away reaction. Formation of toxic chemicals. Overfilling or loss of containment. When is it important? ●​ Receiving chemicals at our site. ●​ Chemical transferring, e.g.: loading chemicals to a tank. ●​ Waste handling operation. Challenges in the field ●​ Lack of knowledge & guidance of the contractor or operator involved. ●​ Safe Line up. ●​ Chemical identification. ●​ Hose Assembly design specifications and identification Preventive Measures ●​ Validate that the right chemical is loaded by a positive identification: analysis of a sample, inline analysis (density), certificate, barcode, clear label. ●​ Have a good procedure in place with check points. ●​ Provide unique coupling for hazardous chemicals (e.g. Chlorine, Nitric Acid, Hydrofluoric Acid) to avoid wrong line-up. ●​ Use colour codes (or bar codes that can be scanned) on pipelines, tubing and connection point. ●​ All chemical transport companies must be ADR, ADN & RID compliant). ●​ Guide contractors well that are involved in (un)loading. ●​ Assure that receiving equipment has sufficient volume available. ●​ Apply Company supervision in all hazardous chemical transfers. ●​ Have a compatibility matrix available to understand the hazards. 26 Uncontrolled copy Process Safety Framework Code: ESG-OM-17 Edition: 0 Avoid run-away reaction Hazards Exothermic reactions could lead to exponential runaways that become hazardous events. When is it important? ●​ Exothermic batch reactions. ●​ Storage of reactive chemicals (e.g.: Acids, Bases, H2O2) ●​ Unexpected Polymerization or Decomposition. ●​ Mixing unstable chemicals. Challenges in the field ●​ Chemistry at increased temperature can be different or unknown to operators. ●​ Cooling can malfunction or might not be able to cope with the exponential increase of the reaction rate. Preventive Measures ●​ Understand the chemistry and side reactions at abnormal conditions like elevated temperature. ●​ Understand the point where cooling can not cope with the exponential heat of the reaction (point of no return). ●​ Assure good design data is available on the heat balance of all the reactions involved (like DSC curves). ●​ Understand the effect of malfunctioning cooling. Have a reactivity matrix available & make sure operators know the critical combinations of chemicals to avoid. ●​ Assure cooling is reliable and have back-up cooling available. ●​ Validate inhibitors are present as applicable. ●​ Have a last line of defence like Interlocks, breaker plates, bunkers. Have an emergency procedure: ●​ Run away in a runaway reaction! 27 Uncontrolled copy Process Safety Framework Code: ESG-OM-17 Edition: 0 Report and manage Process Safety incidents Hazards Acceptance of small leakages, near misses or substandard practices. When is it important? ●​ When related to Safety Critical Equipment. ●​ Small leakages & Activation of barriers. Challenges in the field ●​ No open learning culture that stimulates intervention by all on safety. ●​ Production pressure. ●​ Bad follow-up and feedback on reported items. ●​ Difficult reporting tools. Preventive Measures ●​ Proactively look for indicators or signals that suggest future problems, exploring the causes of changing indicators or unusual situations. ●​ Create a culture where reporting nasty items is considered valuable feedback to improve safety. Have time available for that. ●​ Classify LOPC according to a standard and have a KPI with a target. ●​ Persistently report and record all spills: have an easy database to do so. ●​ Follow-up on reported items and thoroughly investigate all incidents and near-misses to identify root cause and implement corrective action. ●​ Classify LOPC according to a standard and have a KPI with a target. ●​ Ensure workers recognise and report any LOPC event, including TIER 3 & 4 incidents, which are weak signals or leading indicators, that should include: ○​ Small leakages. ○​ Failures of safety critical systems. Activation of a last line of defence like a safety interlock. Fires; liquid hammering; vibrations; corrosion. ○​ Pressure or temperature outside design: like Autorefrigeration. ○​ Locked or car-sealed valves not in the right position. ○​ Long standing or nuisance alarms. ○​ Ignition sources in zoned areas; Atex deficiencies. ○​ Deviation of critical procedures. ●​ Conduct regular safety audits of the PSM-related activities to ensure the effectiveness of the safety measures. ●​ Ensure Preparedness for Process Safety Event 28 Uncontrolled copy Process Safety Framework Code: ESG-OM-17 Edition: 0 ○​ Establish clear evacuation procedures and assembly points ○​ Develop and maintain Emergency Response Plans for PSM events ○​ Conduct regular safety drills 29 Uncontrolled copy Process Safety Framework Code: ESG-OM-17 Edition: 0 5.​ Process Safety Key Performance Indicators As defined in ESG-OM-05 Incident Management and Reporting. Process Safety Incidents are classified as follows: Tier 1 Is a loss of primary containment (LOPC) with the greatest consequences, e.g. fires and explosions causing lost time injuries, one or multiple fatalities or significant financial impact (greater than organisational tolerance levels) or serious environmental impact or harm to the community or substantial reputation impact. Tier 2 LOPC with the lesser consequences, e.g. fires and explosions causing a recordable injury or financial impact (within organisational tolerance levels) or environmental impact or low harm to the community or reputation impact. Tier 3 Typically represents a challenge to the barrier system and near misses, e.g. deviations in safety operational limits, potential LOPC. Tier 4 Typically represents performance of individual components of the barrier system and are comprised of operating discipline and management system performance (e.g. KPI of PSM). Process Safety Incident Rate (PSIR) is calculated as: PSIR: (Total Tier 1 + Tier 2 Count) * 1,000,000 / Hours worked (production activities) 30

Acerinox, S.A. is the holding company of the Acerinox Group. It approves and monitors the strategic lines of the business. It also provides various corporate services (including legal, accounting and advisory services) and manages the financing activities of the Group. The Acerinox Group’s head office is located in Madrid (Spain), where the Parent, Acerinox S.A., is based and where the main decision-making and management bodies convene. The shares of Acerinox, S.A. are listed for trading on the continuous market of the Spanish Stock Exchange, and the Company is part of Spain’s selective IBEX 35 index. At December 31, 2022, the share capital of Acerinox comprised 259,724,345 ordinary shares, each with a nominal value of EUR 0.25. The Annual General Meeting of Acerinox, held on June 16 2022, approved the distribution of a dividend of 0.50 euros per share, which gave rise to shareholder remuneration amounting to EUR 130 million. Direct procurement includes raw materials used and directly integrated into the final product delivered by Acerinox. General procurement, includes all those services and products that are used to manufacture the product. # Acerinox’s Procurement Process In order to optimize the efficiency, effectiveness, transparency and traceability of our processes, we have implemented digital tools that allow us to simplify our work and enable a more agile and effective collaboration with our suppliers. Registration The registration and approval of new suppliers is done through Jaggaer (link). This step is essential to start any relationship with Acerinox. Offer evaluation All bidding, auctions, and RFxs are conducted through Jaggaer, the procurement platform, to ensure transparency and simplicity. An evaluation covering technical aspects and ESG criteria is conducted for each of them. To be awarded, the criteria mentioned on the website must be met. GoSupply registration Once a project or contract has been awarded, it is necessary to be registered on the GoSupply platform. This tool ensures the correct traceability of the supply chain as well as the identification and management of potential and actual risks. Contract signature and/or purchase order Project awards will be formalized through the signing of a contract or order reflecting the scope of the business relationship. Invoicing and payment Invoicing and payment will be made as agreed in the commercial terms. Invoicing will be notified via email and/or regular post. Assessment and performance Suppliers are subject to yearly evaluations on delivery times and quality, product and/or service performance and sustainability performance. The final result will determine whether the product and/or service meet the service level agreements. Audits As part of responsible purchasing management, Acerinox can request on-site and/or online audits that can be carried out either by our company itself or by accredited external auditors. These audits will focus on ESG compliance and/or capacity analysis (verification of capacity, operational flexibility, quality management system...). # Digital procurement tool More transparency, more collaboration [![Jaggaer logo](/es/portal-de-proveedores/.galleries/IMAGENES-Portal-de-Proveedores/Jaggaer-Logo.png "Jaggaer logo")](/en/portal-de-proveedores/jaggaer/ "More information about Jaggaer") Procurement and supplier management platform that allows us to improve onboarding and also optimize the tender processes through automation and data analysis. As a leading company in the stainless steel sector, Acerinox is committed to sustainability, respect and defense of human rights and promotes an integrative corporate culture committed to diversity, equity and inclusion. With our supply chain being a key part of our activity, Acerinox promotes and requires suppliers to adhere to and abide by the same principles. The Acerinox Group's Responsible Procurement Policy and Code of Conduct for Business Partners include the requirements we have established for our suppliers. These documents explain the duties and commitments that are essential for establishing a business relationship with us and therefore are part of our supplier selection process. In a market as **challenging** and changing as today’s market, excellence is a fundamental aspect for our success. This is why it is important to recognize the commitment of the suppliers that have driven our leadership. Suppliers that have demonstrated an outstanding operational performance, a real and tangible commitment to sustainability, and an amazing capacity for adaptation, responding quickly and effectively both to our needs and to market demands. The purpose of the **“Acerinox Supplier of the Year Awards”** is precisely to recognize that talent. We seek to reward partners who have provided us with creative solutions, who compete through innovation, and who understand, like us, that the highest ethical standards are non-negotiable. And, above all, we recognize those who share our vision and want to be relevant players in the future of stainless steel and special alloys”. **Bernardo Velázquez Herreros.** CEO of Acerinox. The “Acerinox Supplier of the Year Awards” are a direct reflection of our operational management model. Through this initiative, which has involved all of the Group’s main manufacturing plants, we highlight strategic collaborations that have provided us with differential value. Our model is structured around a fundamental pillar: the perfect balance between the **autonomy and flexibility** of each of our plants, and the **coordination and efficiency** required by a global market. ## Award categories The award categories have been designed to honor both aspects of this vision: #### 1. **Local Partner Award** Aimed at suppliers who demonstrate a strong commitment to local development. Through this award, we recognize partners that **actively strengthen the industrial sector** in the regions where our plants operate, contributing directly to Acerinox’s “glocal” model. #### 2. **Global Partner Award** This category is awarded to partners capable of working with us on a global scale. We recognize companies with an international presence that ensure **streamlined and adapted local support** in different countries, yet managed through **centralized global coordination**. This synergy is key to our efficiency and competitiveness. ## Evaluation Criteria In both categories, the key points taken into consideration for the awards have been: * **Sustainability****:** The level of development and implementation of their policies, actively promoting ethical and responsible practices. * **Flexibility and Adaptation****:** The support and flexibility demonstrated in adapting to our production and manufacturing processes and challenging situations. * **Operational Improvement****:** The direct and measurable contribution to Acerinox’s efficiency, through digitalization, the optimization of their operations, competitiveness, and innovation. **Recognizing excellence and sharing values of growth: a vision that builds success****.** # We presented the 2025 Supplier of the Year Awards It has been a pleasure to present these awards from our factories in acknowledgement of the commitment of the suppliers that have fueled our leadership. Ms. García Fau holds a Bachelor’s degree in Law and Business Administration from the Comillas Pontifical University (ICADE, E3) and she holds an MBA from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (Sloan, MIT). Ms. García Fau has developed her career in companies such as McKinsey & Co., Goldman Sachs, Telefónica Group and Yell Group. During her professional stage at Telefónica Group, she held several executive responsibilities at TPI Páginas Amarillas, including Chief Financial Officer (CFO) and Managing Director of Corporate Development, while also serving as a member of the Board of Directors for several of its subsidiaries. At Yell, she served as CEO for Spain, Latin America, and the U.S. Hispanic market, a member of its International Executive Committee, and Managing Director of Corporate Development and Global Strategy, with responsibility for digital transformation. Furthermore, she has served on the Advisory Board of Pictet Wealth Management (Iberia). Currently, she serves on the Advisory Board of Fremman Capital and she is an external advisor to the Board of the Cosentino Group. She is also a Trustee of the Comillas (ICAI) University Foundation and member of the Board of Officers of El Círculo de Empresarios. Previously, she was part of the Boards of Directors of Eutelsat, Technicolor, Globalvía, Renovalia Energy, Euskaltel, Merlin Properties, Group Santa Lucía, Finerge and JDE Peets's, NV. Furthermore, she was part of the Advisory Boards of Salesforce and DLA Piper, among others.
